nameStory: The 'bog' in bog cranberry tells you exactly where to find this little beauty - in the acidic, waterlogged soils of peat bogs and wetlands. The 'cranberry' name comes from early European settlers who called these plants 'craneberries' because the curved flower stems looked like the neck and head of a crane bending down to drink.
description: Bog cranberry is a tiny, creeping evergreen shrub that hugs the ground like a living carpet in acidic wetlands. This delicate member of the heath family rarely grows taller than your ankle, spreading by thin, wiry stems that can stretch several feet across the sphagnum moss. Its small, oval leaves are dark green on top with silvery undersides, and in late spring it produces distinctive pink flowers that look like tiny shooting stars. The bright red berries that follow are much smaller than grocery store cranberries but pack a tart punch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink flowers with four swept-back petals that curve dramatically backward, exposing prominent stamens - they look exactly like miniature shooting stars dangling from thread-like stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves about the size of your pinky nail, dark green above with distinctive silvery-white undersides that flash when the wind blows them

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeping, mat-forming shrub that stays very low to the ground, with thin, wiry stems that trail across sphagnum moss like delicate green threads

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries about the size of a pea, much smaller than commercial cranberries, with an intensely tart flavor that makes your mouth pucker

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found growing directly on or nestled into sphagnum moss in acidic bogs, often with your feet getting wet as you search

habitat: Bog cranberry thrives in the acidic, nutrient-poor conditions of sphagnum bogs, fens, and boggy areas around ponds throughout New England's cooler regions. Look for it growing directly on or woven through cushions of sphagnum moss, often alongside pitcher plants, sundews, and Labrador tea. It prefers areas where the soil stays consistently moist or waterlogged, typically in elevations from sea level to mountain bogs.

seasonality.spring: Small pink shooting-star flowers appear in late May through June, dangling from hair-thin stems above the evergreen foliage.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and tiny green berries begin developing, while the distinctive silvery leaf undersides are most noticeable as summer breezes flip the small leaves.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to bright red and remain on the plant, often becoming sweeter after the first frost touches them.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves persist under snow, often taking on reddish tints in the cold, with dried berries sometimes still clinging to stems.

funFact: Bog cranberries are so lightweight and air-filled that they actually bounce when dropped - commercial cranberry growers still use 'bounce boards' to separate the good berries from damaged ones, and bog cranberries bounce even higher than their larger cousins!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with American cranberry, but bog cranberry's leaves are much smaller (pinky-nail sized vs. thumb-nail sized) and the flowers have dramatically swept-back petals like shooting stars rather than American cranberry's more bell-shaped blooms. Memory trick: bog cranberry flowers look like they're 'shooting' backward, while American cranberry flowers hang down like little bells.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this native bog cranberry with the large American cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) that's commercially grown in flooded bogs - they're related but very different in size. The berries from bog cranberry are edible and traditionally used by Indigenous peoples, but they're much more tart than store-bought cranberries.
compareHints: Among its Vaccinium relatives, bog cranberry is distinguished by its extremely small size and creeping habit - while lowbush blueberries also stay low, they form upright clumps rather than trailing mats. The swept-back flower petals are unique among New England Vaccinium species, and unlike blueberries which prefer drier acidic soils, bog cranberry demands the wettest, boggiest conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its Vaccinium cousins, lingonberry is evergreen while blueberries lose their leaves in winter.
Differs from highbush blueberry mainly by size - lowbush stays under 2 feet while highbush can reach 6-12 feet tall.
American cranberry is much more robust than its cousin bog cranberry, with leaves twice the size and significantly larger berries.
Unlike lowbush blueberry which has green leaf undersides and toothed leaf edges, bog bilberry has distinctly pale leaf undersides and smooth-edged leaves.
Among its Vaccinium relatives, northern highbush blueberry is easily the tallest – lowbush blueberry stays under 2 feet, while lingonberry and the various cranberries are ground-hugging plants.
Among New England blueberries, velvetleaf blueberry is the only one with distinctly fuzzy leaves - lowbush and highbush blueberries have smooth, hairless leaves.
Unlike highbush blueberries that grow tall and upright, early lowbush stays under 3 feet and spreads horizontally.
Among New England's blueberries, black highbush stands out for its distinctively dark berries and fuzzy stems and leaves.
Unlike lowbush and highbush blueberries which have stamens that stay tucked inside their flowers, deerberry's stamens prominently stick out like tiny antennae.
Unlike its lowland cousins like lowbush blueberry and highbush blueberry, dwarf bilberry stays extremely small and produces single berries instead of clusters.
Compared to lowbush blueberry, northern blueberry prefers cooler climates and higher elevations, with slightly rounder leaves and often more intense berry flavor.
